ingredients.preparation: myeolchi, the tiny 2–3 cm grade — not the large ones, which want a different dish

ingredients.item: crushed roasted peanuts or walnuts , optional but the classic drinking build

instructions.heading: The dry toast first — the technique
instructions.action: The dry toast first — the technique. Dry pan, medium heat, anchovies tossed for 4–5 minutes until they smell toasted-nutty and turn matte and snap-crisp (break one: it should crack, not bend).
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: the smell shift is unmistakable: from the fish-market jar smell to warm, toasty, almost nut-like. This pre-toast is the difference between crisp-chewy perfection and the tough, faintly damp disappointing version.

instructions.heading: Step 2
instructions.action: Push the anchovies to the pan's side, oil into the empty half, garlic in until it sizzles blond (30 seconds), then the soy, syrup, and gochugaru stirred into the oil — a bubbling glaze — anchovies and nuts tossed through, 1–2 minutes of constant motion as the glaze tightens and coats.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: every anchovy wears gloss, the pan is nearly dry, and a test piece has the target texture: crisp shell, faint chew at the core, sweet-salty-heat. The 60-second window between glazed and tough is the only clock in the recipe — off the heat when they still seem slightly soft, because they crisp further as they cool.

instructions.heading: Step 3
instructions.action: Off the heat: sesame oil and seeds, a final toss, spread on a plate to cool in a single layer (piled hot, they steam each other soft).
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: fully cooled, an anchovy snaps cleanly. The bowl is ready — and it keeps, in a sealed jar, for two to three weeks, which makes it the banchan board's only long-shelf member.

storageNotes: The keeper: 2–3 weeks in a sealed jar at room temperature — the make-ahead banchan for a whole month of grill nights.
Variations: peanuts are the classic partner; a heavier gochugaru hand for the soju table; the same technique on dried shrimp (the smaller cousin, saeu-bokkeum) runs sweeter and faster.
